title: Vayaḥ suparṇāḥ: the seers came to Indra
theme: A Vedic verse in which the seers, like fair-winged birds, come to Indra and ask him to drive away the darkness, fill their sight and set them free.

words.role: in apposition to ṛṣayaḥ, or a simile
words.context: the anonymous commentator: «वय इव पक्षिण इव शीघ्रगमनाः» — like birds, swift

words.meaning: to whom the rite is dear (or: the Priyamedhas)
words.context: the anonymous commentator: «प्रियमेधाः सर्वप्राणिप्रियकृतबुद्धिविशेषाः» — whose minds are set on what is dear to all beings
the anonymous commentator: «ऋषयः सप्तसंख्याकाः» — the seven seers

words.gram: present participle middle, m. nom. pl.
words.context: the anonymous commentator: «नाधमानाः किमपि याचितुकामाः» — wishing to ask for something
the anonymous commentator, reading apadhvāntam with Indra, takes it as ‘cover [us]’: «ऊर्णूहि दिव्यदुकूलादिप्रदानेनाऽऽच्छादय»
the anonymous commentator: «अस्माकं चक्षुः पूर्धि» — fill our eye
the anonymous commentator: «अस्मान्सर्वेभ्यः पापेभ्यो मुमुग्धि मोचय» — release us from all sins

words.role: dative with avabaddhān, as the base’s avagraha and the commentator take it

words.context: the anonymous commentator: «निधयेऽवबद्धानासक्तान्कुरु» — make [us] attached to treasure

sandhi.rule: The Taittirīya recitation writes the visarga before s as ss: vayaḥ suparṇāḥ → vayas suparṇāḥ.

sandhi.type: visarga after ā and after u before a vowel
sandhi.rule: suparṇāḥ + upaseduḥ → suparṇā upaseduḥ: after ā the visarga is dropped before a vowel and the vowels stay apart; upaseduḥ + indram → upasedur indram: after u it becomes r.

sandhi.type: visarga after a before a voiced consonant

sandhi.rule: nidhaye + avabaddhān → nidhaye ’vabaddhān: the a after e is elided, marked by the avagraha.

morphology.note: Imperative 2nd singular of √pṛ, ‘fill’ (classically पूर्धि). The base writes the d doubled after r, a spelling of the recitation text; the Ānandāśrama pariśiṣṭa text and the Tirupati e-text write पूर्धि (see flags).
The base prints अव बद्धान् with a space; the participle with its preverb is given as one word.
Perfect 3rd plural of √sad with upa-, ‘they sat near, approached’ (with the s of the root after the preverb).

translation.literal: The birds, fair-winged, approached Indra — the seers to whom the rite is dear, beseeching: Uncover the darkness, fill the eye, release us, bound to a treasure.
translation.readable: Like fair-winged birds the seers came to Indra, longing, devoted to the rite, and asked: drive the darkness away, fill our sight, and set us free — us who are bound.

anvaya: सुपर्णाः वयः प्रियमेधाः नाधमानाः ऋषयः इन्द्रम् उपसेदुः । ध्वान्तम् अप ऊर्णुहि । चक्षुः पूर्द्धि । निधये अवबद्धान् अस्मान् मुमुग्धि
syntax: A narrative sentence in the perfect (upaseduḥ), whose subject ṛṣayaḥ is described as vayaḥ suparṇāḥ, priyamedhāḥ and nādhamānāḥ; then the seers’ request, three imperatives in a row (apa … ūrṇuhi, pūrddhi, mumugdhi), the last governing asmān … avabaddhān.

ambiguities.note: With apa as the separated preverb of ūrṇuhi the words mean ‘uncover the darkness’. The anonymous commentator instead reads apadhvāntam as describing Indra, ‘free of darkness’ («अपध्वान्तमपगतहृदयान्धकारम्»), and ūrṇuhi as ‘cover us’ with garments.

The letters allow nidhaye ava-baddhān (‘bound to a treasure’), as the base’s avagraha and the anonymous commentator take them, and also nidhayā iva baddhān (‘bound as by a snare’). The edition follows the printed avagraha.
Birds in apposition to the seers, or a simile; the anonymous commentator makes it a simile, ‘swift like birds’.

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: As printed the two lines count 22 and 21 syllables. The second line is one short because mumugdhy asmān joins two vowels; read apart (mumugdhi asmān) it has 22, the regular 11 + 11.

beginner: This is an old Vedic verse placed here among the prayers. It tells a short scene: the seers, like birds with beautiful wings, came to the god Indra and asked him for something. Their request is in three parts: drive away the darkness, fill our eyes, set us free. The anonymous commentator, the only one in this edition who explains the verse, reads it as a mantra for repetition and tells a fuller story: seven seers went up to Indra in heaven, asked for garments, beauty and treasure, received them, and returned to their hermitages. Other readers have taken the darkness and the binding in a more inward sense; the edition reports the commentator’s reading as his.
analogy: Like travellers who arrive at a door at night and ask for three things at once: a light, a clear view, and the untying of their burdens.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: The seers, fair-winged like birds, came to Indra, beseeching; they asked him to uncover the darkness, fill the eye and release them, who are bound.

commentary.q: How does the commentator use it?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator calls it a mantra for repetition, a dialogue between Indra and the seers («सप्तर्षिसंवादकं मन्त्रं»), said for the removal of all sins and for gaining wealth. He completes the story: the seers, made happy by what Indra gave them, came down to the earth and stayed in their hermitages («एवमृषियाचितेनेन्द्रेण दत्तैर्भाग्यैः सुखिताः सन्त ऋषयो भूमिमेत्य स्वाश्रमेषु स्थितवन्त इत्याद्युपाख्यानं पूरयितव्यम्»).

commentary.q: What do they ask for, in his reading?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Garments, beauty and treasure: ‘cover us’ with divine cloth («दिव्यदुकूलादिप्रदानेनाऽऽच्छादय»), ‘fill our eye’ by showing and giving beautiful things, ‘release us from all sins’, and make us ‘attached to treasure’ («अनेकधनरत्नवन्निधियुक्तानस्मान्कुर्वित्यर्थः»). He takes apadhvāntam as describing Indra: «अपध्वान्तमपगतहृदयान्धकारम्».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The base writes अप ध्वान्तमूर्णुहि and निधयेऽव बद्धान् with spaces; the letters can be divided more than one way (see ambiguities). The base doubles the d of pūrdhi (पूर्द्धि), where both other witnesses and the commentator write पूर्धि.

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this text is in the edition’s sources: Raṅgarāmānuja’s is not available, and the commentaries present (the anonymous bhāṣya, Sāyaṇa, Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara) are ritual and Vedic explanations, not school readings. Only the anonymous commentator explains this verse in the edition’s sources.

contemporary.text: The seers’ request names exactly what they lack: light, sight, release. Being able to say precisely what one needs is often the first part of receiving it. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: If you could ask for three things in the words of this verse, what would ‘darkness’, ‘eye’ and ‘bound’ mean for you?
reflect.deeper: The commentator reads the requests as worldly goods. What would change if they were read as requests for understanding?
reflect.practice: Write down one thing you need help with, as plainly as the seers ask.

references.text: The verse is also found in the Ṛgveda (10.73.11); the edition’s Ṛgveda source has only the first maṇḍala, so it is not cited as a checked parallel.
No comment of Sāyaṇa or Bhāskara on this anuvāka is in the edition’s files.

flags.note: पूर्द्धि (base) against पूर्धि (the Ānandāśrama pariśiṣṭa text and the Tirupati e-text agree): the collation leaves it for review. The base’s spelling is kept; the form is the same imperative.
The commentator’s reading (apadhvāntam of Indra; ūrṇuhi ‘cover’; nidhaye avabaddhān ‘attached to treasure’) differs from the plain sense of the words as divided in the base.
Only one commentary explains this anuvāka in the edition’s sources.
